name: Neck training harness
lead: A neck training harness is a head strap or cap, connected by a chain or strap to a weight plate or other resistance, that loads the neck muscles through flexion, extension and side flexion. People use it to build a thicker, stronger neck, which changes how the head, jaw and shoulders read against each other in profile, in photographs and on camera. Wrestlers, boxers and other combat-sport athletes have long trained the neck, and the harness has been adopted by lifters and appearance-focused trainees as an inexpensive way to apply progressive overload to the muscles of the neck.

The neck is a group of ordinary skeletal muscles, including the sternocleidomastoid at the front and sides and the trapezius and splenius muscles at the back, and these are the muscles that give a developed neck its visible width.[13][14] Average neck circumference is reported as roughly 38.7 cm for men and 33.3 cm for women, with the difference attributed mainly to body composition, muscle mass and testosterone's influence on neck muscle growth.[14] Proponents say adding neck muscle makes the neck look wider relative to the head and balances the jaw, traps and shoulders; looksmax.org users discuss it in those terms.[12][18]

Published research on neck training covers healthy volunteers, people with neck pain, and athletes in collision and combat sports. Small trials in healthy participants have measured strength gains and muscle cross-sectional area, a sports-medicine review and expert consensus have examined neck training as a way to lower head acceleration in sport, and electromyography studies have compared the muscle activation produced by different resistance equipment.[1][3][5][7] No controlled trial has used a head harness specifically or measured how a thicker neck changes perceived facial attractiveness.

angle.text: A harness lets a trainee add external load to neck movements the way a barbell does for other muscles. As the neck muscles grow, the neck gets wider, which proponents say balances the head and jaw and fills out the line from the ears to the shoulders in profile and on camera.

paras: Harnesses generally consist of a padded leather or nylon cap or strap that fits around the head, with a chain or strap that attaches to a weight plate or dumbbell. Some versions combine a head strap with a chin cup, and others are built as a full cap that spreads pressure across the skull. A user lies on a bench or sits and moves the head against the load; the same movements can be loaded with resistance bands, a partner's hands, a towel held against the forehead or a dedicated neck machine.

The sternocleidomastoid is one of the largest and most superficial neck muscles. It runs from the sternum and clavicle up to the mastoid process behind the ear, flexes the neck when both sides act together, and tilts and rotates the head when one side acts alone; it is visible and palpable at the side of the neck.[13] The posterior triangle of the neck also contains the trapezius, splenius capitis and levator scapulae, and the scalenes sit deeper at the side.[14] Neck flexion, extension and side flexion against resistance load these groups.

The working assumption in strength training is that muscles grow when they meet progressively greater resistance, with enough volume and recovery between sessions.[15] Resistance-training reviews describe a positive relationship between volume and hypertrophy, and report that two weekly sessions produced more growth than one.[15] Trainees who use a harness apply that framework to the neck by gradually increasing the plate load or the number of repetitions.

A 2013 randomised pilot trial in 26 healthy women compared two ten-week neck programmes performed twice weekly, one using resistance training alone and one combining resistance with proprioceptive work. Strength gains did not differ significantly between groups, but the increase in muscle cross-sectional area was greater in the combined group, ranging from about 19% to 32% across three muscle groups, versus about 1.5% to 13% for resistance alone.[3]

Training also changes how the nervous system controls the neck. A 2013 trial in Spine used transcranial magnetic stimulation and found that only specific neck strength training, not coordination training, produced a lasting increase in motor evoked potential amplitude, about 67% above baseline for up to seven days.[4] A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis in PLOS ONE pooled 14 articles from 2,110 citations on exercise and neuromuscular function in chronic neck pain and reported moderate-certainty evidence that craniocervical flexion training, alone or with resistance training, induces neural adaptations; the meta-analysis found reduced sternocleidomastoid activity after exercise compared with control interventions.[7]

A randomised trial of 180 women with chronic neck pain compared high-intensity isometric strength training and dynamic endurance training with a control group, with follow-up at 2, 6 and 12 months. The greatest strength gains occurred in the first two months and continued up to 12 months, the strength group gained the most at every follow-up, and the control group changed little.[6] Reviews of deep cervical flexor training have examined its effects on impaired physiological function in chronic neck pain.[8]

A 2008 study in the Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research compared neck muscle activation in 17 asymptomatic adults using surface electromyography during exercise with elastic Thera-Band resistance and with Cybex machine resistance. Machine resistance produced considerably higher muscle activation than the elastic band, which the authors suggested made the band better suited to rehabilitation and the machine to injury-prevention work; they also noted that the load placed on passive spinal structures is unknown, so prescription should be careful.[5]

Controlled data on visible neck thickening come mainly from the 2013 pilot trial of healthy women, which measured cross-sectional area by imaging after ten weeks.[3] Proponents describe visibly thicker necks after months of training, and looksmax.org users share routines and photographs.[11][12][19] No controlled trial has measured the effect of neck size on facial or jaw appearance or on how attractive observers rate the result.

A 2025 systematic review and Delphi consensus study in the British Journal of Sports Medicine searched databases to September 2024 for neck-training interventions in collision, combat and motor sport, found 21 eligible papers with widely varying interventions, and then convened 18 international experts, who produced 57 consensus statements across five categories: contextual factors, periodisation, training adaptations, content and athlete adherence.[1] A 2025 review of head acceleration during soccer headers included 60 studies,[2] and a 2026 review of concussion prevention in adult football found five eligible studies, two of them head-neck training interventions, rated fair or poor quality, none of which reported statistically significant directional effects.[9]

A 2024 single-arm prospective cohort study in Cureus followed 162 collegiate athletes in high-concussion-risk sports through a 12-week programme using a portable neck-exercise device. Cervical strength rose in all teams, with the most consistent gains in flexion and extension, and the athletic department's rate of head and neck injuries including concussions fell to 6.6 percent, which the authors described as the lowest recorded there.[10] A preliminary study of neck training and neck pain in military aircrew exposed to high G forces has also been reported.[17]

The cervical spine contains the spinal cord, nerve roots and vertebral arteries, and heavy loads, jerky repetitions or poor control are generally described as raising the risk of muscle strain and nerve irritation. Training guidance commonly advises light initial resistance and gradual progression, and people with prior neck injury, disc problems or dizziness are generally advised to consult a clinician before loading the neck. The 2008 electromyography study noted that the stress placed on passive spinal structures by neck exercise is not known.[5] These precautions come from general clinical practice and not from trials of the harness.

Causes of neck pain listed in anatomy references include whiplash and other soft-tissue injury, cervical disc herniation, spinal stenosis and osteoarthritis.[14] A related note in the same reference is that a larger neck circumference is associated with cardiometabolic risk, but this reflects fat distribution in population studies and is a separate matter from muscle added through training.[14]

Neck work takes several forms besides the harness. The wrestler's bridge is a position in which the body is arched with weight resting on the head or shoulders and the feet, used in wrestling and grappling to escape from the bottom and also as an exercise position.[16] Manual resistance, towel resistance, bands and neck machines load the same movements. Looksmax.org users discuss neck curls in several directions, and some say slow, stretch-focused repetitions can be enough without added weight.[11][12][20]

In appearance and physique communities neck training is presented as a way to broaden the neck, which proponents say balances the head and improves the look of the jaw, shoulders and traps in profile and on camera. The harness is described as an inexpensive route to progressive overload compared with machine-based neck equipment. Looksmax.org has several threads on the topic, including a posted training guide, a thread asking about results after two months, and threads asking for photographs of the jaw area after neck training.[11][12][18][19]

Common questions in these threads include how often to train, whether training one side more will leave the neck asymmetrical, and why changes can be slow to appear. Users also tie neck size to the idea of a 'high T' physique, a slang expression for looking as if testosterone levels are high.[12][20]

Typical points compared between products are padding and fit of the head cap, strap or chain length, the weight-bearing attachment point and whether the strap is adjustable for head size. Prices commonly fall in the range of about $20 to $40.

No studies found testing the harness itself. Research on neck training in general includes a randomised pilot trial of neck resistance training in 26 healthy women measuring strength and muscle cross-sectional area,[3] a 180-woman trial of strength versus endurance neck training in chronic neck pain,[6] a trial of neck training and corticomotor excitability,[4] an electromyography comparison of band and machine resistance in 17 adults,[5] a meta-analysis of exercise and neuromuscular function in chronic neck pain,[7] and sports reviews and a cohort study of neck training to reduce head acceleration events and concussion.[1][2][9][10]

timeline.event: A 180-woman randomised trial in chronic neck pain reports strength gains after high-intensity and endurance neck training, followed for 12 months.[6]
Electromyography study compares neck muscle activation with band and machine resistance in 17 adults.[5]

A randomised pilot trial measures neck strength and muscle cross-sectional area after ten weeks of training in 26 healthy women, and a Spine trial reports lasting corticomotor changes after specific neck strength training.[3][4]
BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders publishes a systematic review of deep cervical flexor training in chronic neck pain.[8]
A PLOS ONE meta-analysis of exercise and neuromuscular function in neck pain, and a Cureus cohort study of a 12-week neck programme in 162 collegiate athletes.[7][10]
British Journal of Sports Medicine publishes a systematic review and 18-expert Delphi consensus on neck training to reduce head acceleration events.[1]
A review of concussion prevention in adult football maps sparse evidence on head-neck training.[9]

lore.intro: Neck training is a recurring topic on looksmax.org, where users discuss it as a way to build a thicker neck that they say complements the jaw and physique, and share routines, questions and photographs.[11][12][18][19][20]

claims.claim: A thicker, stronger neck improves physique, posture and a 'high T' look
claims.believers: A looksmax.org guide says a thicker and stronger neck goes hand in hand with the physique, helps posture over time and makes one look like a 'high T mogger'; it describes neck extension and flexion exercises done with a towel over the head.[12]
claims.experts: Studies have measured neck strength, muscle cross-sectional area and electromyographic activity, and training for neck pain or head-impact reduction; none assessed perceived attractiveness or hormonal appearance.[3][5][6][1] A randomised trial in healthy women compared two ten-week neck programmes for strength and muscle cross-sectional area.[3]

claims.claim: Neck exercises can be done without added weight if done slowly with a stretch
claims.believers: A reply in the guide thread says one does not even need weight if training slowly and prioritising stretch, which should aid hypertrophy; another adds tension and reps with good technique.[12]
claims.experts: Published neck-training studies used resistance, isometric or proprioceptive protocols; no study has tested slow bodyweight neck work for hypertrophy.[3][5][6] The 2008 electromyography study found that lighter elastic resistance produced low muscle activation compared with machine resistance.[5]

claims.claim: Training the neck three times a week for two months should show visible results
claims.believers: A looksmax.org user reports training his neck about three times weekly for two months and seeing no results, and asks whether his routine is wrong.[11]
claims.experts: A ten-week trial in healthy women measured neck strength and muscle cross-sectional area after twice-weekly training.[3] A randomised trial in women with chronic neck pain reported that most strength gains came in the first two months and continued up to 12 months.[6]

claims.claim: Training one side more than the other will make the neck asymmetrical
claims.believers: In a looksmax.org thread a user asks whether doing neck curls up, down and to the side could leave him asymmetrical if one side is trained more, and a reply says that an overtrained side will become asymmetrical.[20]
claims.experts: General strength-training references describe muscle growth as following progressive loading of the trained muscle.[15] No published study has examined cosmetic asymmetry from uneven neck training.

claims.claim: Neck training changes how the jaw area looks in photographs
claims.believers: Looksmax.org has threads titled around neck training for better looks and jaw-area pictures, where users compare photographs of the neck and jaw region.[18][19]
claims.experts: A neck circumference reference attributes average sex differences mainly to body composition, muscle mass and testosterone's effect on neck muscle growth.[14] No controlled trial has tested whether neck training alters perceived jaw definition or facial attractiveness.

claims.claim: Stronger neck muscles reduce concussion risk in athletes
claims.believers: Coaches and athletes in collision sports use neck strengthening for this purpose, and a Cureus cohort study of 162 collegiate athletes reported the lowest head and neck injury rate in the department's history after a 12-week neck programme.[10]
claims.experts: A 2025 systematic review and Delphi consensus found 21 interventions of widely varying design and produced 57 consensus statements,[1] while a 2026 review of adult football found two head-neck training studies of fair or poor quality with no statistically significant directional effects.[9]
